Q9191525.summary: Christ stands beside Mena, abbot of the monastery at Bawit, resting his right arm gently around the abbot's shoulder while holding a jeweled Gospel book in his left hand. With large, wide-open eyes and simplified, frontal forms, the panel expresses a warm companionship between the Lord and his servant. Often called the 'Icon of Friendship', it is among the oldest surviving Coptic icons and a beloved image of Christ's protective care.
facts: Inscriptions identify the figures: 'Savior' beside Christ, and 'Apa Mena, proeistos' ('Father Mena, superior') beside the abbot.
Its date is debated: some scholars, such as Hans Belting, place it in the 6th century, while the Louvre dates it to the 8th century.
The icon measures about 58.5 × 57.7 cm and is marked by vertical cracks; found at Bawit in 1901–02, it was stolen from the excavation, then bought and given to the Louvre in 1918.
Its image of Christ's arm around a friend has made it a symbol of ecumenical friendship, popularized especially by the Taizé Community.
Q9191525.notes: Dating differs: the Louvre gives 8th century (700–799); English Wikipedia says second half of the 6th century. The Louvre date is used. The Louvre currently lists it as not on display.

cur:manuscripts-khludov-iconoclast-counc.summary: In the margin at the left, the patriarch Nikephoros stands holding an icon of Christ, while at the foot of the page an iconoclast assembly sits around an enthroned ruler and one figure reaches toward a medallion icon of Christ beside a vessel of whitewash. The page contrasts reverence for Christ's image with its destruction, illustrating the psalm's rejection of 'the assembly of evildoers'.
facts: The Commons description identifies the scene as the iconoclast council of 815 under Emperor Leo V, with Patriarch Theodotos, and the icon being destroyed by John the Grammarian and Antony of Syllaion.
According to Wikipedia, some scholars attribute the psalter to the Stoudios monastery, others to imperial workshops soon after the restoration of icons in 843.
cur:manuscripts-khludov-iconoclast-counc.notes: Identification of the figures follows the Commons description; the lower scene is badly worn. Psalm number and folio not verified.

cur:objects-kells-south-cross.summary: At the centre of the weathered head on the west face of this cross Christ is shown crucified, his arms outstretched along the arms of the cross, with figures pressing in from either side. The cross is dedicated by its inscription to Saints Patrick and Columba, the patrons of Irish Christianity and of the Columban monastery of Kells. Though worn, the carving still conveys the Irish devotion to Christ crucified at the heart of the monastic enclosure.
facts: It is the oldest of the five high crosses at Kells and bears an inscription naming Saints Patrick and Columba, from which it takes its alternative name (photographer's documentation).
Wikipedia notes that the round tower and high crosses at Kells are a National Monument of Ireland.
cur:objects-kells-south-cross.notes: The image is a weathered close view from below; the identification of the central figure as the crucified Christ follows the usual west-face scheme but the photograph is not sharp.

walters:W.44.152R.summary: Within a gold-and-blue initial D, two haloed figures sit side by side on one bench, each holding a closed book: God the Father and Christ, illustrating the opening words of Psalm 109 (110), 'The Lord said to my Lord: sit at my right hand.' The Father raises his hand to his breast and the Son lifts his in speech, as if in conversation. It is one of the original 13th-century historiated initials of this Flemish Psalter.
facts: The Psalter's ten historiated initials, original to the book, mark a ten-part division at Psalms 1, 26, 38, 51, 52, 68, 80, 97, 101 and 109; this is the last of them (fol. 152r).
Verse 1 of this psalm is quoted in the New Testament (Matthew 22:44, Acts 2:34–35, Hebrews 1:13) and applied to Christ, which is why the two divine Persons are shown enthroned together.
The manuscript was later owned by the Munich dealer Jacques Rosenthal and by Léon Gruel in Paris before Henry Walters acquired it.

walters:W.44.152R.notes: Worklist year 750 was a parsing error for '3rd quarter 13th century'. Unlike the prefatory miniatures, the historiated initials are original to the 13th-century Psalter.

feat:archbishops-chapel-christ-warrior.summary: Over the entrance to the bishops' private chapel, a beardless Christ wears the armor and cloak of a Roman general, carrying a cross over his shoulder like a standard and holding an open book. Beneath his feet he tramples a lion and a serpent, symbols of evil. It is a bold image of Christ the victor, made for orthodox bishops in a city ruled by the Arian Gothic king Theodoric.
facts: The open book reads EGO SUM VIA VERITAS ET VITA: 'I am the way, the truth and the life'.
Trampling the lion and the serpent fulfills Psalm 91:13: 'You will tread on the lion and the adder'.

Built under Bishop Peter II shortly after he took office in 494/495, the chapel was originally dedicated to Christ the Saviour; its strongly anti-Arian imagery was made for the orthodox (Nicene) bishops.
It is the smallest of Ravenna's famous mosaic monuments, reached through the Archiepiscopal Museum, and is considered the only early Christian private oratory to survive to the present day.
